claim: PMB-resistant variants of Acinetobacter baumannii produce outer membrane vesicles (OMVs).
source: PMB-resistant variants and many clinical isolates also appeared to produce outer membrane vesicles (OMVs).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract based on observations from the study.

claim: Upregulation of the pmr operon is linked to overproduction of OMVs in PMB-resistant A. baumannii.
source: Genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses revealed that upregulation of the pmr operon and decreased membrane-linkage proteins (OmpA, OmpW, and BamE) are linked to overproduction of OMVs, which also promoted enhanced biofilm formation.
evidence: Multi-omics analyses (genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic) showed this relationship.

claim: Decreased membrane-linkage proteins (OmpA, OmpW, and BamE) are linked to overproduction of OMVs in PMB-resistant A. baumannii.
source: Genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses revealed that upregulation of the pmr operon and decreased membrane-linkage proteins (OmpA, OmpW, and BamE) are linked to overproduction of OMVs, which also promoted enhanced biofilm formation.

claim: Overproduction of OMVs promotes enhanced biofilm formation in PMB-resistant A. baumannii.
source: Genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses revealed that upregulation of the pmr operon and decreased membrane-linkage proteins (OmpA, OmpW, and BamE) are linked to overproduction of OMVs, which also promoted enhanced biofilm formation.
evidence: Multi-omics analyses and biofilm assays showed this relationship.

claim: OMVs from PMB-resistant A. baumannii variants protect PMB-susceptible A. baumannii from PMB.
source: The addition of OMVs from PMB-resistant variants into the cultures of PMB-susceptible A. baumannii and the clinical isolates protected these susceptible bacteria from PMB.
evidence: Experimental addition of OMVs to susceptible strains demonstrated protection.

claim: OMVs completely protect in vitro human gut microbiomes against PMB treatment under anaerobic conditions.
source: Taxonomic profiling of in vitro human gut microbiomes under anaerobic conditions demonstrated that OMVs completely protected the microbial community against PMB treatment.
evidence: Taxonomic profiling experiments showed complete protection of the microbial community.

claim: OMVs increase the mortality rate of Galleria mellonella larvae by protecting A. baumannii from PMB.
source: A Galleria mellonella-infection model with PMB treatment showed that OMVs increased the mortality rate of larvae by protecting A. baumannii from PMB.
evidence: In vivo infection model demonstrated increased larval mortality with OMV addition.

claim: OMVs released from A. baumannii function as decoys against PMB.
source: Taken together, OMVs released from A. baumannii functioned as decoys against PMB.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches including protection assays and binding studies.

claim: Pathogenic Acinetobacter baumannii strains cause urinary tract infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia.
source: Pathogenic Acinetobacter baumannii strains cause urinary tract infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia (Wright et al., 2014).

claim: Multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (MRAB) are resistant to various antibiotics including sulbactam and tigecycline.
source: The incidence and prevalence of multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (MRAB), which are resistant to various antibiotics including sulbactam and tigecycline, threaten the effective prevention and treatment of MRAB-related infections (Brauers et al., 2005; Perez et al., 2007; Alsan and Klompas, 2010).

claim: Carbapenem antibiotics such as imipenem, meropenem, and doripenem are mainly used to treat severe MRAB infections.
source: The broad-spectrum β-lactam carbapenem antibiotics, such as imipenem, meropenem, and doripenem, are mainly used to treat severe MRAB infections (Papp-Wallace et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2012).

claim: MRAB clonal complex 92 contains the blaOXA-23 gene encoding a carbapenem-hydrolyzing class D β-lactamase.
source: Unfortunately, studies have reported the spread of MRAB clonal complex 92, which contains the blaOXA-23 gene encoding a carbapenem-hydrolyzing class D β-lactamase (Antunes et al., 2014; Yoon et al., 2017).

claim: ISAba I upstream of blaOXA-type genes allows A. baumannii strains to transmit antibiotic resistance genes through horizontal gene transfer.
source: Mobile genetic elements, particularly ISAba I upstream of the blaOXA-type genes, allow A. baumannii strains to transmit the antibiotic resistance (AR) gene to other bacteria and the environment through horizontal gene transfer (Bahador et al., 2015).

claim: Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) is a top-priority pathogen requiring new antibiotics or combination therapies.
source: Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) is a top-priority pathogen, for which new antibiotics or combination therapies are desperately needed (Shlaes and Bradford, 2018).

claim: Colistin and polymyxin B are used to treat MRAB and CRAB infections despite their adverse effects.
source: Lack of an efficacious treatment for MRAB and CRAB infections has caused a reversion to initial treatments involving drugs that are considered dated now, such as colistin and polymyxin B (PMB), despite the adverse effects of these drugs (Velkov et al., 2013).

claim: Polymyxins kill Gram-negative bacteria by binding to the bacterial outer membrane.
source: Polymyxins are cationic polypeptide antibiotics that specifically kill Gram-negative bacteria by binding to the bacterial outer membrane (OM).
evidence: Established mechanism of action cited in the literature.

claim: Polymyxins interact with negatively charged lipopolysaccharide (LPS) components by displacing positively charged ions such as Mg2+ and Ca2+.
source: These last-resort antimicrobial agents interact with the negatively charged lipopolysaccharide (LPS) components of the OM by displacing positively charged ions, such as Mg2+ and Ca2+. Consequently, the integrity of the cell membrane is impaired, leading to cell death (Jeannot et al., 2017; Moffatt et al., 2019).

claim: Modification of lipid A in LPS by pmrCAB and arnBCADTEF gene products is a primary mechanism of resistance to polymyxins.
source: Modification of lipid A in LPS by pmrCAB and arnBCADTEF gene products, which are modulators of the bacterial OM surface charge and permeability, is generally recognized as a primary mechanism of resistance to polymyxins (Trent et al., 2001; Olaitan et al., 2014; Jeannot et al., 2017).

claim: The pmrCAB and arnBCADTEF operons regulated by PmrAB modify lipid A by adding 4-amino-4-deoxy-l-arabinose (LAra4N) and phosphoethanolamine (PetN), respectively.
source: The pmrCAB and arnBCADTEF operons regulated by a PmrAB two-component system modify lipid A by adding 4-amino-4-deoxy-l-arabinose (LAra4N) and phosphoethanolamine (PetN), respectively (Kline et al., 2008; Arroyo et al., 2011; Pelletier et al., 2013).

claim: A. baumannii lacks genes for LAra4N biosynthesis and uses PetN addition as the main polymyxin-resistance mechanism.
source: Because A. baumannii lacks the genes for the biosynthesis of LAra4N, it uses PetN addition as the main polymyxin-resistance mechanism (Gerson et al., 2019).

claim: In PMB-resistant A. baumannii, mutant PmrB protein is autophosphorylated, phosphorylating PmrA which upregulates PmrC.
source: In PMB-resistant A. baumannii, the mutant PmrB protein is autophosphorylated, consequently phosphorylating the cytoplasmic transcriptional regulator PmrA. Phosphorylated PmrA then upregulates the PetN transferase PmrC and prevents PMB binding to lipid A (Cannatelli et al., 2014).

claim: Lipid A modifications decrease the negative charge of the cell membrane, reducing PMB binding affinity.
source: These modifications in lipid A decrease the negative charge of the cell membrane, reducing the membrane-binding affinity of PMB. Consequently, the cell is protected from the PMB-mediated disruption of its membrane and survives (Trimble et al., 2016).

claim: In some A. baumannii clinical isolates, eptA gene expression is activated by ISAba I sequence, contributing to PMB resistance.
source: In some A. baumannii clinical isolates, expression of the eptA gene is activated by the adjacent ISAba I sequence, and the gene product PmrC homolog contributes to PMB resistance (Trebosc et al., 2019).

claim: E. coli producing outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) can survive in the presence of PMB.
source: Interestingly, E. coli producing outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) can survive in the presence of PMB (Manning and Kuehn, 2011; Kulkarni et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2018).

claim: Gram-negative bacteria release OMVs with diameters of 20–400 nm composed of phospholipids, outer membrane proteins, and LPSs.
source: Gram-negative bacteria release OMVs with diameters of 20–400 nm to their environments. These vesicles are composed of phospholipids (PLs), outer membrane proteins (OMPs), and LPSs or lipooligosaccharides (LOS), but also contain periplasmic proteins and cell wall components (Roier et al., 2016a).

claim: Modulation of peptidoglycan (PG) cross-links is associated with membrane stability and rigidity.
source: Modulation of peptidoglycan (PG) cross-links is associated with membrane stability and rigidity (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).

claim: Approximately one-third of Lpp anchored to the outer cell membrane are covalently cross-linked with PGs.
source: Approximately one-third of the alpha-helical OM lipoprotein Lpp (also known as Braun's lipoprotein) anchored to the outer cell membrane are covalently cross-linked with PGs through connection between C-terminal lysine residue of Lpp and the diaminopimelic acid (meso-DAP) site of PG (Dramsi et al., 2008).

claim: Reduction in Lpp production disrupts PG cross-linkage on the membrane, contributing to OMV formation.
source: Reduction in Lpp production disrupts the cross-linkage of PG on the membrane, thereby significantly contributing to the formation of OMVs (Wessel et al., 2013).

claim: Differential expression of OmpA can modulate OMV excretion.
source: Differential expression of OM protein A (OmpA), which is a β-barrel porin that non-covalently interacts with the meso-DAP site of PG, can modulate OMV excretion (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).

claim: Absence of inner membrane proteins such as Tol and NlpA can enhance OMV production.
source: Many mutant studies have shown that the absence of inner membrane (IM) proteins, such as the Tol component of the Tol-Pal system and NlpA, can enhance OMV production (Bernadac et al., 1998; Toyofuku et al., 2015).

claim: High periplasmic turgor pressure from accumulated misfolded proteins, nucleotide fragments, or PG debris facilitates OMV production.
source: Production of OMVs is also facilitated by a high periplasmic turgor pressure, which occurs when misfolded proteins, nucleotide fragments, or PG debris accumulate in the periplasm (Brown et al., 2015).

claim: In Haemophilus influenzae, OMVs are released when PL transporters of the VacJ/Yrb ABC transport system are not produced.
source: Additionally, in Haemophilus influenzae, OMVs are also released by PLs that accumulate on the OM when the PL transporters of the VacJ/Yrb ABC transport system (also known as the Mla system) are not produced (Roier et al., 2016b).

claim: Changes in membrane fluidity and rigidity determined by PL compositions affect OMV production.
source: Changes in membrane fluidity and rigidity, determined by the compositions of acyl chains and head groups of PLs, affect OMV production (Mashburn-Warren et al., 2008).

claim: The proportion of saturated fatty acids is higher in OMVs than in cellular membranes.
source: The proportion of saturated fatty acids appears to be higher in OMVs than in cellular membranes (Baumgarten et al., 2012).

claim: OMVs from pathogenic bacteria have physiological functions including biofilm formation, cell–cell communication, secretion of virulence factors, and survival under antibiotic stress.
source: In pathogenic bacteria, these spherical OMVs formed by various routes can have many different physiological functions, including biofilm formation, cell–cell communication, secretion of virulence factors, and survival under antibiotic stress (Toyofuku et al., 2015; Bonnington and Kuehn, 2016).

claim: OMVs have attracted interest as putative vaccine agents or vehicles for drug delivery.
source: OMVs have attracted interest as putative vaccine agents or vehicles for drug delivery (Jan, 2017).

claim: OMVs can reduce the effectiveness of antibiotics and other bactericidal agents.
source: They can reduce the effectiveness of antibiotics and other bactericidal agents, thereby posing a serious threat to the treatment of bacterial infections (Koeppen et al., 2016; Jan, 2017).

claim: OMVs of β-lactam-resistant E. coli are enriched with proteins involved in degrading β-lactam antibiotics.
source: For example, the OMVs of β-lactam-resistant E. coli are enriched with proteins involved in degrading β-lactam antibiotics in comparison with those of susceptible bacteria (Kim et al., 2018).

claim: OMV supplementation of microbial cultures increases microbial resistance to antimicrobial peptides.
source: Accordingly, OMV supplementation of microbial cultures increases the microbial resistance to antimicrobial peptides. Similarly, hypervesiculating mutants show increased resistance (Manning and Kuehn, 2011).

claim: OMVs from A. baumannii possess various virulence factors such as OmpA, proteases, phospholipases, superoxide dismutase, and catalase.
source: OMVs from A. baumannii are known to possess various virulence factors such as OmpA, proteases, phospholipases, superoxide dismutase, and catalase (Kwon et al., 2009).

claim: PMRLow strain has a MIC of 4 μg/mL, which is 2-fold higher than Lab-WT.
source: Consequently, strains that had 2-fold (MIC, 4 μg/mL) and 64-fold (MIC, 128 μg/mL) higher PMB resistance than Lab-WT were generated (low and high PMB resistance, PMRLow and PMRHigh, respectively) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: PMRHigh strain has a MIC of 128 μg/mL, which is 64-fold higher than Lab-WT.
source: Consequently, strains that had 2-fold (MIC, 4 μg/mL) and 64-fold (MIC, 128 μg/mL) higher PMB resistance than Lab-WT were generated (low and high PMB resistance, PMRLow and PMRHigh, respectively) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: PMRHigh strain has a lower growth rate (1.386 ± 0.17 h−1) than Lab-WT (2.081 ± 0.92 h−1) and PMRLow (1.985 ± 0.86 h−1).
source: The PMRHigh strain had a lower growth rate (1.386 ± 0.17 h−1) than both Lab-WT (2.081 ± 0.92 h−1) and PMRLow (1.985 ± 0.86 h−1) strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pmrC gene expression is 1.2-fold higher in PMRLow and 4-fold higher in PMRHigh compared to Lab-WT in the absence of PMB.
source: Expression analyses of the pmrC gene, which encodes a PetN transferase in the absence of PMB, showed 1.2- and 4-fold higher expression in PMRLow and PMRHigh strains, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: qRT-PCR expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average negative surface charge of PMRLow decreased from −27 mV (Lab-WT) to −20 mV.
source: The zeta-potential analyses suggested that the average negative surface charge of PMRLow and PMRHigh decreased from −27 mV (Lab-WT) to −20 mV and −10 mV, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: The average negative surface charge of PMRHigh decreased from −27 mV (Lab-WT) to −10 mV.
source: The zeta-potential analyses suggested that the average negative surface charge of PMRLow and PMRHigh decreased from −27 mV (Lab-WT) to −20 mV and −10 mV, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: PMRHigh strain produces twofold more biofilm than Lab-WT strain.
source: Quantification of biofilm formation using the crystal violet assay also indicated that the PMRHigh strain produced more biofilm (twofold higher) than the Lab-WT strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Crystal violet assay measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Addition of OMVs derived from PMRHigh increased the initial stage of Lab-WT biofilm formation.
source: Interestingly, addition of OMVs derived from PMRHigh increased the initial stage of Lab-WT biofilm formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Biofilm formation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: PMRLow and PMRHigh strains are resistant only to polymyxins, but not to nine other tested antibiotics of different classes.
source: The PMRLow and PMRHigh strains were resistant only to polymyxins, but not to the other nine tested antibiotics of different classes, including meropenem, rifampicin, chloramphenicol, and ampicillin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: MIC testing of multiple antibiotics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: OMV production is twofold higher in PMRHigh than in Lab-WT.
source: OMV production appeared to be twofold higher in PMRHigh than in Lab-WT, and the treatment with 1/2 MIC PMB (1 or 128 µg/mL, respectively) caused increased OMV production as quantified using the lipophilic dye FM4-64 (Figure 1C).
evidence: FM4-64 dye quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with 1/2 MIC PMB caused increased OMV production in both Lab-WT and PMRHigh strains.
source: OMV production appeared to be twofold higher in PMRHigh than in Lab-WT, and the treatment with 1/2 MIC PMB (1 or 128 µg/mL, respectively) caused increased OMV production as quantified using the lipophilic dye FM4-64 (Figure 1C).
evidence: FM4-64 dye quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PMRHigh strain produces markedly larger and greater amounts of OMVs than Lab-WT strain.
source: We observed markedly larger and greater production of OMVs in the PMRHigh strain than in our Lab-WT strain using TEM (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: TEM observations shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Dissociated OMVs from PMRHigh are larger and become entangled with other OMVs through hairy structured materials.
source: Dissociated OMVs from PMRHigh were larger and became entangled with other OMVs through hairy structured materials (Figure 1E).

claim: The main peak of Lab-WT lipid A was measured at 1490 m/z, corresponding to bis-phosphorylated penta-acylated lipid A.
source: The main peak of Lab-WT was measured at 1490 m/z, corresponding to bis-phosphorylated penta-acylated lipid A (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: In PMRHigh strain, the predominant lipid A spectrum was measured at 1490 m/z, followed by 1630 m/z.
source: In the PMRHigh strain, the predominant spectrum was also measured at 1490 m/z, followed by 1630 m/z, which is predicted to be the peak when a PetN and a hydroxyl group were attached to the dominant lipid A (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The 1630 m/z peak in PMRHigh is predicted to be lipid A with an attached PetN and a hydroxyl group.
source: In the PMRHigh strain, the predominant spectrum was also measured at 1490 m/z, followed by 1630 m/z, which is predicted to be the peak when a PetN and a hydroxyl group were attached to the dominant lipid A (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry analysis and interpretation shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The phenylalanine peak at 1002 cm−1 is similar in both Lab-WT and PMRHigh strains.
source: This phenylalanine peak at 1002 cm−1 appeared to be similar in both strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Raman spectroscopy analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Raman peak corresponding to phospholipids (at 1334, 1445, and 1666 cm−1) increased notably in PMRHigh.
source: However, the Raman peak corresponding to PL (at 1334, 1445, and 1666 cm−1) increased notably in PMRHigh (Figure 2C).
evidence: Raman spectroscopy analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The intensity of the Raman peak at 1243 cm−1 assigned to an amide III β-sheet was higher in PMRHigh.
source: The intensity of the other prominent peak at 1243 cm−1 assigned to an amide III β-sheet was higher in resistant strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Raman spectroscopy analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Principal coordinate analysis using Raman spectra revealed that Lab-WT and PMRHigh cluster into two groups with 38.2% explanatory power.
source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) using the collected Raman spectra of bacterial cells revealed that dispersion of individual dots was clustered into two groups, with 38.2% explanatory power, although some dots were in shared areas between Lab-WT and PMRHigh (Figure 2D).

claim: Lab-WT strains are more heterogeneous than PMRHigh strains based on individual cell heterogeneity analysis.
source: Individual cell heterogeneity analysis showed that Lab-WT strains were more heterogeneous than resistant strains, suggesting that PMRHigh strains were specifically adapted and unified by PMB stress (Figure 2E).

claim: PMRHigh strains were specifically adapted and unified by PMB stress.
source: Individual cell heterogeneity analysis showed that Lab-WT strains were more heterogeneous than resistant strains, suggesting that PMRHigh strains were specifically adapted and unified by PMB stress (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inference from heterogeneity analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A. baumannii ATCC 17978 strain possesses a single chromosome and two plasmids, pAB1 (13,408 bp) and pAB2 (11,302 bp).
source: It has been known that A. baumannii ATCC 17978 strain possesses a single chromosome and two plasmids, namely pAB1 (13,408 bp) and pAB2 (11,302 bp).
evidence: Known from literature and confirmed by WGS analysis.

claim: The small plasmid pAB2 (11,299 bp, three bases deleted) was detected only in PMRHigh.
source: The same small plasmid, pAB2 (11,299 bp, three bases were deleted), was detected only in the PMRHigh.

claim: The large plasmid pAB1 was missing in both PMRLow and PMRHigh evolved strains.
source: The large plasmid was missing in both evolved strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: WGS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The chromosome sizes of ATCC 17978, PMRLow, and PMRHigh are 3,976,747 bp, 3,971,618 bp, and 3,955,017 bp, respectively.
source: The chromosome sizes of ATCC 17978, PMRLow, and PMRHigh were 3,976,747 bp, 3,971,618 bp, and 3,955,017 bp, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: WGS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two chromosomal regions mostly annotated as hypothetical proteins were lost during adaptive evolution of PMRLow and PMRHigh strains.
source: Two chromosomal regions mostly annotated as hypothetical proteins were lost during adaptive evolution of PMRLow and PMRHigh strains (Supplementary file 1c).

claim: All 20 antibiotic-resistant genes and 78 IS elements remain unchanged in both evolved strains.
source: All 20 antibiotic-resistant genes and 78 IS elements remain unchanged in both evolved strains (Supplementary file 1d, e).

claim: PMRHigh strain has mutations in surE, fimT, ftsL (nonsense mutation), udg, xerD, and fabH (nonsense mutation).
source: In the PMRHigh strain, mutations were found in the protein damage repair gene surE, fimbrial gene fimT, cell division-related gene ftsL (nonsense mutation), DNA repair gene udg, DNA integration gene xerD, and fatty acid synthesis-related gene fabH (nonsense mutation) (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: WGS analysis shown in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PMRLow has a point mutation in pmrB with amino acid substitution at N353I.
source: Additionally, comparative genomic analysis between Lab-WT and PMRHigh strains revealed point mutations in the pmrB gene of the PMRHigh strain. PmrB was the protein that showed different mutations in the PMRLow and PMRHigh strains, with amino acid substitutions at N353I and T2351, respectively (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: WGS comparative analysis shown in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PMRHigh has a point mutation in pmrB with amino acid substitution at T2351.
source: Additionally, comparative genomic analysis between Lab-WT and PMRHigh strains revealed point mutations in the pmrB gene of the PMRHigh strain. PmrB was the protein that showed different mutations in the PMRLow and PMRHigh strains, with amino acid substitutions at N353I and T2351, respectively (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: WGS comparative analysis shown in Supplementary file 1a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutations N353I and T2351 in PmrB are known to increase pmrC expression, resulting in PetN modification of lipid A.
source: The mutations in N353I and T2351 in PmrB are known to increase the expression of the pmrC, resulting in PetN modification of lipid A (Adams et al., 2009).

claim: 250 genes were upregulated and 166 genes were downregulated in PMRHigh compared to Lab-WT without PMB exposure.
source: Our RNA-seq analysis showed that 250 and 166 genes were up- and downregulated, respectively, in PMRHigh in comparison with the Lab-WT strain without PMB exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 89.16% of all genes showed no change at the transcriptional level between PMRHigh and Lab-WT.
source: In addition, 89.16% of all genes showed no change at the transcriptional level.

claim: The aldB gene encoding an aldehyde dehydrogenase showed a 3.43-fold increase in PMRHigh compared to Lab-WT.
source: The highly upregulated gene, encoding an aldehyde dehydrogenase (aldB), showed a 3.43-fold increase in the PMRHigh in comparison with that in the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 8 of the 16 most upregulated genes in PMRHigh were hypothetical proteins.
source: 8 of the 16 most upregulated genes were hypothetical proteins, and the remaining genes were annotated as a glutamin-(asparagin)-ase (ansB), poly-beta-1,6-N-acetyl-d-glucosamine N-deacetylase (pgaB), ribosomal protein (rpmI), and an ABC transporter glutamine-binding protein (glnH) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PMRHigh strain showed upregulation of both pmrA and pmrC genes.
source: The PMRHigh strain showed upregulation of both pmrA and pmrC genes encoding a transcriptional regulator and a PetN transferase, respectively, which evidently affects the membrane charge leading to PMB resistance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The most downregulated genes in PMRHigh (except hypothetical genes) were ompA and bamE encoding outer membrane proteins.
source: Notably, the most downregulated genes except the hypothetical gene were related to two genes encoding the OMPs ompA and bamE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lack of OmpA in the outer membrane promotes bacterial OMV production.
source: Lack of OmpA in the OM is known to promote bacterial OMV production (Schwechheimer et al., 2014).

claim: BamE binds specifically to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) in the outer membrane.
source: The bamE, encoding a β‐barrel assembly machine E, was shown to bind specifically to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) in the OM (Knowles et al., 2011).

claim: Both OmpA and BamE are determinants for cell shape and outer membrane integrity.
source: Both OmpA and BamE are determinants for cell shape and OM integrity (Ryan et al., 2010; Choi and Lee, 2019).

claim: qRT-PCR confirmed that pmr and pgaB genes showed more than fourfold higher expression in PMRHigh.
source: An additional qRT-PCR assay confirmed that the pmr and pgaB genes showed more than fourfold higher expression, but all membrane-linkage-related genes (ompA, bamE, lpp, and mlaC) were downregulated in PMRHigh (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).

claim: All membrane-linkage-related genes (ompA, bamE, lpp, and mlaC) were downregulated in PMRHigh.
source: An additional qRT-PCR assay confirmed that the pmr and pgaB genes showed more than fourfold higher expression, but all membrane-linkage-related genes (ompA, bamE, lpp, and mlaC) were downregulated in PMRHigh (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).

claim: 29 genes were upregulated and 12 genes were downregulated in hypervesiculation conditions.
source: Our RNA-seq analyses confirmed that 29 and 12 genes were up- and downregulated, respectively, in the hypervesiculation conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: RNA-seq comparative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ribosomal proteins (rplW and rplO) and chaperons (groL) were upregulated in hypervesiculation conditions.
source: High levels of gene expression involved in stress response and survival were also predominant in the transcriptomic analysis, in which ribosomal proteins (rplW and rplO) and chaperons (groL) were upregulated in the hypervesiculation conditions (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis listed in Supplementary file 1g.

claim: The pgpA gene encoding a lipid phosphatase was upregulated in hypervesiculation conditions.
source: The pgpA gene encoding a lipid phosphatase was also upregulated, which can dephosphorylate phosphatidylglycerophosphate to form PG, a major constituent in OMVs (Supplementary file 1g, Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis listed in Supplementary file 1g and cited literature.

claim: Increased levels of PG in the outer membrane induce changes in membrane integrity, causing higher OMV production.
source: Increased levels of PG in the OM induced changes in membrane integrity, causing higher OMV production (Sohlenkamp and Geiger, 2016).

claim: Commonly downregulated genes in hypervesiculation conditions included membrane-associated genes (mlaC, ompA, lpp, and bamE).
source: Notably, several genes belonging to the pmr and pga operons are included among the commonly upregulated gene categories, and the commonly downregulated genes included important membrane-associated genes (mlaC, ompA, lpp, and bamE) (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: RNA-seq comparative analysis listed in Supplementary file 1g.

claim: 43 out of 61 up- or downregulated proteins in OMVs were identified by MALDI-TOF analysis.
source: 43 out of the 61 up- or downregulated proteins were designated with the MS-Fit program by using the NCBInr and UniPortKB databases, and 18 spots were not identified (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Proteomics analysis listed in Supplementary file 1h.

claim: Commonly identified OMV components showed increased production of PmrC, alanine racemase (Alr), and PgaB.
source: The commonly identified OMV components harbored several proteins that were noted in our RNA-seq analyses for OMV biogenesis, showing increased production (PmrC, alanine racemase [Alr], and PgaB) and decreased production (OmpA and OmpW, elongation factor Tu [TufB]).

claim: Commonly identified OMV components showed decreased production of OmpA, OmpW, and elongation factor Tu (TufB).
source: The commonly identified OMV components harbored several proteins that were noted in our RNA-seq analyses for OMV biogenesis, showing increased production (PmrC, alanine racemase [Alr], and PgaB) and decreased production (OmpA and OmpW, elongation factor Tu [TufB]).

claim: A. baumannii OMVs contain cytoplasmic cargo proteins such as ribosomal proteins and Ef-Tu.
source: Interestingly, A. baumannii OMVs also contained many cytoplasmic cargo proteins such as ribosomal proteins and Ef-Tu, similar to the OMVs from other bacteria (Dallo et al., 2012; Deo et al., 2018).

claim: Elongation factor (Ef-Tu) is one of the most abundant proteins (>20%) in bacteria.
source: Elongation factor (Ef-Tu), observed in our proteomics analyses, is one of the most abundant proteins (>20%) in bacteria and has a canonical role in translation.

claim: Ef-Tu is found on the surface of bacterial outer membranes, suggesting a possible noncanonical function.
source: However, it is also found on the surface of bacterial OMs, which suggests a possible noncanonical function on the membrane (Widjaja et al., 2017; Harvey et al., 2019).

claim: OMV production appeared to be 1.5- to 2-fold higher in PMRHigh than PMRLow or Lab-WT as quantified by FM4-64 dye.
source: OMV production appeared to be 1.5- to 2-fold higher in PMRHigh than PMRLow or Lab-WT, as quantified by using the lipophilic dye FM4-64 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: FM4-64 dye quantification shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Total protein, DNA, and LPS amounts in OMVs were higher in PMRHigh than Lab-WT.
source: Total protein, DNA, and LPS amounts in OMVs collected from the same amounts of cell cultures were higher in PMRHigh than Lab-WT (Figure 4B–D).

claim: When pmrB gene was deleted in Lab-WT, OMV biogenesis was reduced (0.3-fold).
source: Furthermore, when the pmrB gene was deleted in Lab-WT, OMV biogenesis was reduced (0.3-fold) (Figure 4A–D), indicating that OMV production is impaired in the absence of PmrB.

claim: An extra copy of pmrBH gene increased OMV production in Lab-WT.
source: This finding was supported by our observation in which an extra copy of pmrBH gene increased OMV production in Lab-WT (Figure 4A–D).

claim: The ΔftsL, Δudg, Δlpp, and ΔmlaC mutants exhibited higher OMV production.
source: However, the ΔftsL, Δudg, Δlpp, and ΔmlaC mutants exhibited higher OMV production (Figure 4A–D).

claim: OMV production was reduced when the pgaB gene was deleted in Lab-WT.
source: As expected from our omics data, OMV production was reduced when the PNAG transporter-related gene, pgaB, was deleted in Lab-WT (Figure 4A–D).

claim: The MIC of the pmrB-deleted strain (ΔpmrB) was reduced.
source: The MICs of the pmrB-deleted strain (ΔpmrB) appeared to be reduced (Figure 4E).

claim: Introduction of the complementary pmrB gene to Lab-WT increased the MIC.
source: Introduction of the complementary pmrB gene to Lab-WT (Lab-WT + pRK-pmrB) increased the MIC, whereas the empty vector (pRK) did not affect the MIC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Complementation experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The MICs of ΔftsL, Δudg, Δlpp, and ΔpgaB remained unchanged compared to Lab-WT.
source: The MICs of ΔftsL, Δudg, Δlpp, and ΔpgaB remained unchanged in comparison to that of Lab-WT (Figure 4E).

claim: Dansyl-PMB was less bound to PMRHigh cells than Lab-WT cells at their respective PMB MICs.
source: Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) images revealed that dansyl-PMB was less bound to PMRHigh cells than Lab-WT cells at their respective PMB MICs (2 or 4 µg/mL) due to the fact that the PmrC-driven lipid A modification of PMRHigh cells decreased PMB binding to OMs (Figure 5C).

claim: Dansyl-PMB directly binds to purified OMVs of the PMRHigh strain.
source: The lipid-selective dye (FM4-64) and dansyl-PMB were employed to visualize binding of PMB to purified OMVs of the PMRHigh stain (Figure 5D). Our data showed that the two dyes exhibited overlapping images, which clearly demonstrated the direct binding of PMB to OMVs.

claim: Higher OMV producers among clinical isolates show higher protection rates against PMB in the early stationary phase.
source: Although direct correlations between the MIC and OMV production could not be identified under our tested conditions due to the same reasons we provided earlier, higher OMV producers could show higher protection rates against PMB in the early stationary phase (Figure 6A).
evidence: Analysis of 40 clinical isolates shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Addition of PMRHigh-derived OMVs to five randomly chosen MDR strains enhanced microbial survival in the presence of PMB.
source: Interestingly, addition of PMRHigh-derived OMVs to the growth cultures of five randomly chosen MDR strains (Supplementary file 1i; F-1025, F-1208, F-1379, F-1410, and F-1629) enhanced the microbial survival in the presence of PMB (Figure 6B).

claim: OMV-driven protection under PMB conditions is applicable to other Gram-negative bacteria including P. aeruginosa PAO1, P. putida KT2440, E. coli K12, and A. oleivorans DR1.
source: PMB MIC tests were performed using four additional Gram-negative bacteria (P. aeruginosa PAO1, Pseudomonas putida KT2440, E. coli K12, and Acinetobacter oleivorans DR1) and the protective roles of their OMVs were tested (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Our data suggested that OMV-driven protection under PMB conditions could be applicable to other Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: Protection assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PMB-treated fecal microbiota sample showed a 10^4-fold reduction in aerobic bacterial cells compared to the control.
source: The PMB-treated sample showed a 104-fold reduction in aerobic bacterial cells than the control, and the OMV plus PMB sample showed similar levels of cell counts as the control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Microbiota analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The OMV plus PMB sample showed similar levels of cell counts as the control in fecal microbiota experiments.
source: The PMB-treated sample showed a 104-fold reduction in aerobic bacterial cells than the control, and the OMV plus PMB sample showed similar levels of cell counts as the control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Microbiota analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of OMVs extracted from PMRHigh strain protected the bacterial community from PMB under anaerobic conditions.
source: Our taxonomic profile, along with rarefaction curves and the PCoA 3D plot, revealed that addition of OMVs extracted from the PMRHigh strain protected the bacterial community from PMB under our tested anaerobic conditions, resulting in recovery of a similar microbial composition (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—source data 1).

claim: The total 16S rDNA genes per dried gram in the PMB-added sample decreased by ~16% compared to the 5 days incubated control sample.
source: The total 16S rDNA genes per dried gram in the PMB-added sample (145,311 copies/dried gram) decreased by ~16% in comparison with that in the 5 days incubated control sample (173,403 copies/dried gram), while the corresponding value in the OMV-added sample was reduced by 14% (149,643 copies/dried gram) (Figure 7A).

claim: The PMB-exposed fecal microbiota sample showed 75% lower 16S rDNA copies corresponding to the Enterococcus faecium group than the control.
source: Surprisingly, the PMB-exposed sample showed significantly reduced numbers of 16S rDNA copies corresponding to the Enterococcus faecium group belonging to Gram-positive bacteria (75% lower than the control) and recovery of the E. faecium group occurred in the OMV-added PMB sample (Figure 7A).

claim: Recovery of the E. faecium group occurred in the OMV-added PMB sample.
source: Surprisingly, the PMB-exposed sample showed significantly reduced numbers of 16S rDNA copies corresponding to the Enterococcus faecium group belonging to Gram-positive bacteria (75% lower than the control) and recovery of the E. faecium group occurred in the OMV-added PMB sample (Figure 7A).

claim: No growth inhibition with PMB was observed in aerobically grown Enterococcus type strains (E. faecium and E. faecalis).
source: No growth inhibition with PMB was observed in both aerobically grown Enterococcus type strains (E. faecium and Enterococcus faecalis).

claim: Severe growth retardation with PMB was observed in the anaerobic culture of E. faecium.
source: Interestingly, severe growth retardation with PMB was especially observed in the anaerobic culture of E. faecium (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1).

claim: PMRHigh induced faster death of all tested G. mellonella larvae within 72 hr compared to Lab-WT.
source: Comparison of the mortality rates demonstrated that PMRHigh, which possessed higher virulence than Lab-WT, induced faster death of all tested larvae within 72 hr (Figure 7E).
evidence: G. mellonella infection model shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In the presence of PMB, only 10% of G. mellonella larvae infected with PMRHigh died within 24 hr.
source: In the presence of PMB, only 10% of the G. mellonella larvae infected with PMRHigh died within 24 hr, but 80% of the larvae died when OMVs were included (Figure 7E).
evidence: G. mellonella infection model shown in Figure 7E.

claim: 80% of G. mellonella larvae infected with PMRHigh died within 24 hr when OMVs were included with PMB.
source: In the presence of PMB, only 10% of the G. mellonella larvae infected with PMRHigh died within 24 hr, but 80% of the larvae died when OMVs were included (Figure 7E).
evidence: G. mellonella infection model shown in Figure 7E.

claim: OMVs increased the mortality rate of G. mellonella larvae by protecting A. baumannii from PMB.
source: This experiment suggested that A. baumannii survived longer due to the protective effect of OMVs against PMB, leading to the higher mortality of G. mellonella.
evidence: Inference from G. mellonella infection model shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Production of OMVs has been linked to quorum-sensing, antibiotic resistance, and biofilm formation in pathogenic bacteria.
source: Production of OMVs has been linked to many important cellular behaviors, including quorum-sensing, AR, and biofilm formation in pathogenic bacteria (Florez et al., 2017).

claim: OMV biogenesis is linked to elevated hydrophobicity of the cell surface in P. putida, causing greater biofilm formation.
source: OMV biogenesis was thought to be also linked to the elevated hydrophobicity of the cell surface in P. putida, which caused greater biofilm formation (Baumgarten et al., 2012).

claim: OMVs produced by A. baumannii have a virulence factor (OmpA) and an antibiotic-resistance factor (AmpC).
source: Interestingly, the OMVs produced by A. baumannii have been shown to have a virulence factor (OmpA) and an antibiotic-resistance factor (AmpC) (Weber et al., 2017).

claim: OMVs released from CRAB are responsible for horizontal transfer of the carbapenem-resistance-related gene blaNDM-1 to carbapenem-susceptible A. baumannii.
source: Interestingly, OMVs released from CRAB could be responsible for the horizontal transfer of the carbapenem-resistance-related gene blaNDM-1 to carbapenem-susceptible A. baumannii (Chatterjee et al., 2017).

claim: K. pneumoniae strains have outer membranes and larger OMVs with different lipid compositions under PMB treatment, contributing to low PMB permeability.
source: Notably, Klebsiella pneumoniae strains had OMs and larger OMVs harboring different lipid compositions under PMB treatment, which might contribute to the low permeability of PMB (Jasim et al., 2018).

claim: Reduced LptA connections lead to overproduction of OMVs.
source: A recent study has shown that reduced LptA connections lead to overproduction of OMVs (Falchi et al., 2018).

claim: Disruption of the Mla complex system results in hypervesiculation by accumulation of glycerophospholipids in the outer leaflet.
source: Disruption of the Mla complex system, which transports mislocalized OM glycerophospholipids back to the IM, results in hypervesiculation by accumulation of glycerophospholipids in the outer leaflet (Kamischke et al., 2019).

claim: The Bam complex mediates the folding and insertion of outer membrane proteins into the membrane.
source: The Bam complex is an OM complex that mediates the folding and insertion of OM proteins into the membrane (Malinverni and Silhavy, 2011).

claim: DolP promotes proper folding of BamA and plays a role in outer membrane integrity.
source: DolP, a lipoprotein, is known to promote proper folding of BamA, one of the essential subunits of the BAM complex, which might also play a role in OM integrity (Ranava et al., 2021).

claim: Deletion of bamE in E. coli or S. enteritidis results in more severe defects in outer membrane and lower OM protein levels than loss of bamC.
source: Deletion of bamE in E. coli or in Salmonella enteritidis results in a more severe defect in OM and lower OM protein levels than does loss of bamC (Sklar et al., 2007; Fardini et al., 2009).

claim: OMVs can be generated when decreased cross-links between the outer membrane, peptidoglycan, and inner membrane occur.
source: Taken together, the accumulated data suggest that OMVs can be generated when decreased cross-links between the OM, PG, and IM occur in the bacterial membrane.
evidence: Summary of literature and experimental findings.

claim: Antibiotic-induced genomic alterations including deletions, rearrangements, and amplification have been reported in laboratory-evolved antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains.
source: It is worth noting that antibiotic-induced genomic alterations including deletions, rearrangements, and amplification have been reported in many laboratory-evolved antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains (Sandegren and Andersson, 2009).

claim: Several laboratory-evolved antibiotic-resistant E. coli strains carry more than 20 mutations.
source: Several laboratory-evolved antibiotic-resistant E. coli strains also appeared to carry more than 20 mutations (Maeda et al., 2020).

claim: Tetracycline-induced genome rearrangements led to the loss of 6.1 kb having seven full-length and two truncated genes in E. coli strains.
source: Tetracycline-induced genome rearrangements led to the loss of 6.1 kb having seven full-length and two truncated genes in E. coli strains (Hoeksema et al., 2018).

claim: Norfloxacin-treated E. coli had ~11.5 kb deletions possibly through IS1-mediated recombination.
source: Norfloxacin-treated E. coli had ~11.5 kb deletions possibly through IS1-mediated recombination (Long et al., 2016).

claim: Bacterial OMVs contain inner membrane proteins as well as cytoplasmic proteins.
source: Several other data have also shown that bacterial OMVs contained IM proteins as well as cytoplasmic proteins (Nagakubo et al., 2019).

claim: OMV production through explosive cell lysis in P. aeruginosa includes cytosolic components of cells.
source: The unusual OMV biogenesis recently identified in a P. aeruginosa model system has clearly shown that OMV production through explosive cell lysis ended up including several cytosolic components of cells (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).

claim: Explosive cell lysis induced by phage-derived endolysin leads to the presence of cytoplasmic proteins and DNA in OMVs.
source: Explosive cell lysis induced by phage-derived endolysin burst the outer and IMs, leading to the presence of cytoplasmic proteins and DNA in OMVs (Turnbull et al., 2016).

claim: PQS and MucD are not required for cycloserine-induced OMV formation in P. aeruginosa, indicating multiple pathways for OMV biogenesis.
source: Two known mechanistic factors (PQS and MucD) for OMV production were not required for cycloserine-induced OMV formation in P. aeruginosa, indicating the existence of multiple pathways for OMV biogenesis (Macdonald and Kuehn, 2013).

claim: OMVs have been shown to protect bacterial cells against several classes of antibiotics and physical and chemical stresses.
source: OMVs have been shown to protect bacterial cells against several classes of antibiotics and physical and chemical stresses (Kulkarni et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016).

claim: The decoy activity of OMVs was proposed in an E. coli model under membrane-active antibiotics such as colistin and melittin.
source: The decoy activity of OMVs was proposed in an E. coli model under membrane-active antibiotics such as colistin and melittin (Kulkarni et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2018).

claim: Polymyxins can bind to teichoic acid, a negatively charged compound in the outer membrane of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Recently, more studies suggested that polymyxins can bind to teichoic acid, which is a negatively charged compound in the OM of Gram-positive bacteria (Brown et al., 2013; Rudilla et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020).

claim: V. cholerae cells use hyperproduction of OMVs to increase their colonization and adaptation during mammalian infection.
source: Likewise, Vibrio cholerae cells use hyperproduction of OMVs to increase their colonization and adaptation during mammalian infection (Zingl et al., 2020).

claim: OMVs induced by the pga operon can stimulate the production of broad antimicrobial antibodies against P. aeruginosa in a mouse infection model.
source: Interestingly, the OMVs induced by the pga operon can stimulate the production of broad antimicrobial antibodies against P. aeruginosa in a mouse infection model (Stevenson et al., 2018).
